docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
TLS is a security protocol that protects application communication using authentication, encryption, and integrity mechanisms.

Status: 🟡 Learning Last reviewed: 2026-10-23 Confidence: Beginner

docs.title: What Is TLS?
docs.text:
TLS stands for:

Transport Layer Security

TLS provides security for application communication over a network.

In HTTPS:

HTTP
 ↓
TLS
 ↓
TCP
 ↓
IP

TLS is not limited to HTTP.

Other application protocols can also use TLS.

docs.title: Why Does TLS Exist?
docs.text:
A network path can involve multiple systems:

Client
   ↓
Router
   ↓
ISP
   ↓
Internet Infrastructure
   ↓
Server

Without cryptographic protection, communication could potentially be:

  • observed
  • modified
  • impersonated

TLS addresses these risks by providing:

Confidentiality
Integrity
Authentication

docs.title: Confidentiality
docs.text:
Confidentiality protects data from unauthorized reading.

Conceptually:

Plaintext
   ↓
Encrypt using session key
   ↓
Ciphertext
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Decrypt
   ↓
Plaintext

The network carries protected data rather than the original plaintext.

docs.title: Integrity
docs.text:
Integrity ensures that protected data cannot be modified unnoticed.

If encrypted traffic is changed in transit, cryptographic integrity mechanisms allow the receiver to detect that the data is no longer valid.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Authentication allows a client to verify the identity of the server.

TLS commonly uses certificates for server authentication.

Conceptually:

Server
   ↓
Certificate
   ↓
Client validates identity

docs.title: Symmetric Encryption
docs.text:
Symmetric cryptography uses the same shared secret key for encryption and decryption.

Conceptually:

Shared Secret Key
      ↓
    Encrypt
      ↓
  Ciphertext
      ↓
    Decrypt
      ↓
Shared Secret Key

Advantages:

  • computationally efficient
  • suitable for large amounts of data

Challenge:

How do two parties securely establish the shared key?

TLS solves this during the handshake.

docs.title: Asymmetric Cryptography
docs.text:
Asymmetric cryptography uses a key pair:

Public Key
Private Key

The public key can be shared.

The private key must remain secret.

Conceptually:

Public Key
     ↕
Private Key

The keys are mathematically related.

TLS uses public-key cryptography primarily for:

  • authentication
  • digital signatures
  • key-establishment mechanisms

depending on the TLS version and negotiated algorithms.

docs.title: Why TLS Uses Both
docs.text:
Public-key cryptography is useful for authentication and securely establishing shared secrets.

Symmetric cryptography is much more efficient for bulk traffic.

Therefore:

TLS Handshake
     ↓
Public-Key / Key-Agreement Operations
     ↓
Shared Session Keys
     ↓
Symmetric Protection
     ↓
Application Traffic

Important

TLS does not normally encrypt every application byte using the server's private key.

That is a common misunderstanding.

docs.title: TLS Handshake
docs.text:
The TLS handshake establishes secure communication before protected application traffic is exchanged.

A simplified mental model:

Client                         Server
  |                              |
  | ------ ClientHello ------->  |
  |                              |
  | <----- ServerHello --------  |
  | <----- Certificate --------  |
  |                              |
  |  Validate Certificate        |
  |                              |
  | <---- Key Agreement ------>  |
  |                              |
  |    Shared Keys Derived       |
  |                              |
  | ==== Protected Traffic ====  |

Actual TLS 1.3 messages and ordering are more detailed.

For initial learning, understand the purpose rather than memorizing packets.

docs.title: ClientHello
docs.text:
The client begins the TLS handshake by sending a ClientHello.

It can include information such as:

  • supported TLS versions
  • cryptographic algorithm options
  • key-agreement information
  • extensions
  • server name information

Mental model:

Client:
Here is what I support.

docs.title: ServerHello
docs.text:
The server responds with a ServerHello.

It selects compatible connection parameters from what the client supports.

Simplified:

Client supports:
A
B
C

Server chooses:
B

The server also participates in key agreement and provides authentication information.

docs.title: Certificate Exchange
docs.text:
The server normally provides a certificate chain.

The client validates it.

Conceptually:

Server Certificate
       ↓
Hostname valid?
       ↓
Date valid?
       ↓
Trusted chain?
       ↓
Signature valid?
       ↓
Continue handshake

If validation fails, the connection may be rejected or the user may receive a security warning.

docs.title: Key Agreement
docs.text:
The client and server perform cryptographic operations allowing both sides to derive shared secrets.

Modern TLS commonly uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman-style key exchange.

At this stage, understand only the result:

Client
   +
Server
   ↓
Shared Session Secrets

The secrets are not simply transmitted as plaintext across the network.

docs.title: Session Keys
docs.text:
After the handshake, both sides derive session keys.

These keys are used to protect application data.

Conceptually:

TLS Handshake
      ↓
Session Keys
      ↓
HTTP Request
      ↓
Protected Data
      ↓
Network

Session keys are efficient for ongoing communication.

docs.title: TLS and HTTP
docs.text:
TLS does not understand business concepts such as:

GET /users
POST /orders
404 Not Found

Those belong to HTTP.

TLS protects the bytes representing those messages.

Conceptually:

HTTP
→ application semantics

TLS
→ security

TCP
→ reliable transport

IP
→ routing

docs.title: SNI
docs.text:
SNI stands for:

Server Name Indication

A single server or IP address can host multiple HTTPS domains.

Example:

203.0.113.10

├── api.example.com
├── shop.example.com
└── blog.example.com

The server needs to know which hostname the client wants so it can present the appropriate certificate.

The client can provide the server name during TLS setup.

Conceptually:

Client:
I want api.example.com
        ↓
Server:
Use certificate for api.example.com

docs.title: Why SNI Is Useful
docs.text:
Without hostname information, a server hosting many HTTPS domains on one address would have difficulty choosing the correct certificate before HTTP begins.

Remember:

TLS handshake
happens before
HTTP Host processing

SNI helps solve this.

docs.title: TLS 1.2 vs TLS 1.3
docs.text:
At a high level:

TLS 1.3 simplifies and modernizes the handshake compared with TLS 1.2.

Benefits include:

  • removal of outdated algorithms
  • fewer handshake round trips in common cases
  • modern cryptographic defaults
  • improved security design

Do not memorize detailed packet flows yet.

For now:

TLS 1.3
→ newer
→ simpler
→ stronger defaults
→ more efficient handshake

docs.title: Lab 1 — Inspect TLS with curl
docs.text:
Run:

curl -v https://example.com

Look for TLS-related output.

Try to identify:

TCP Connection
     ↓
TLS Negotiation
     ↓
HTTP

docs.title: Lab 2 — Use OpenSSL
docs.text:
Run:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com

Look for:

  • negotiated TLS version
  • certificate chain
  • certificate subject
  • issuer
  • connection details

docs.title: Lab 3 — Check Negotiated TLS Version
docs.text:
Depending on your OpenSSL version:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com

Look for output similar to:

Protocol
Cipher

Do not memorize cipher names yet.

docs.title: Common Problems
docs.text:
TLS failures may be caused by:

Expired certificate
Hostname mismatch
Unsupported TLS version
Untrusted issuer
Incomplete certificate chain
Incorrect server configuration
Clock/time problems

A useful debugging flow:

Can TCP connect?
      ↓
Does TLS handshake start?
      ↓
Certificate received?
      ↓
Hostname valid?
      ↓
Dates valid?
      ↓
Chain trusted?
      ↓
Compatible TLS algorithms?

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Important TLS practices include:

  • use supported modern TLS versions
  • disable deprecated protocols
  • protect private keys
  • use valid certificates
  • validate certificates correctly
  • do not bypass certificate verification in production
  • rotate keys/certificates appropriately
  • keep TLS libraries patched

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
TLS introduces:

  • handshake latency
  • cryptographic computation

Performance can be improved using:

  • connection reuse
  • TLS session resumption
  • modern TLS versions
  • efficient certificate chains
  • appropriately configured infrastructure

For production systems, security should not be disabled merely to remove TLS overhead.

docs.title: TLS Is Not HTTP
docs.text:
TLS provides security.

HTTP provides application semantics.

docs.title: Private Key Is Not Shared
docs.text:
The server's private key must remain secret.

It is not sent to clients during normal TLS operation.

docs.title: TLS Does Not Encrypt Everything with the Private Key
docs.text: TLS establishes shared session keys and then uses efficient symmetric protection for application traffic.

docs.title: TCP Does Not Provide TLS Security
docs.text:
TCP provides reliable transport.

TLS provides cryptographic security.

docs.text:
TLS is a security protocol that protects communication between applications over a network.

It authenticates the server using certificates, performs cryptographic key agreement, and derives shared session keys.

Those session keys are then used to efficiently protect application traffic using symmetric cryptography.

In HTTPS, TLS sits between HTTP and TCP and protects HTTP communication without changing HTTP's application semantics.

docs.title: UDP
docs.text: UDP is a connectionless transport protocol that sends independent datagrams without providing TCP-style delivery or ordering guarantees.

docs.title: What Is UDP?
docs.text:
UDP stands for User Datagram Protocol.

It is a transport-layer protocol used to send independent messages called datagrams between network endpoints.

A simplified model:

Application
   ↓
UDP Datagram
   ↓
IP
   ↓
Network
   ↓
Destination

Unlike TCP, UDP does not establish a persistent transport connection before sending data.

docs.title: Why Does UDP Exist?
docs.text:
Not every application requires TCP's reliability mechanisms.

Some applications care more about:

  • low overhead
  • low latency
  • timely delivery
  • application-controlled reliability
  • simple message-oriented transport

Examples can include:

  • DNS queries
  • real-time media
  • online games
  • telemetry
  • QUIC-based protocols

UDP provides a simpler transport mechanism for these situations.

docs.title: Core Properties
docs.text:
UDP is generally:

Connectionless
Datagram-oriented
No built-in delivery guarantee
No built-in ordering guarantee
No built-in retransmission
Low protocol overhead

docs.title: Connectionless Communication
docs.text:
UDP does not perform a TCP-style three-way handshake before sending data.

Conceptually:

Sender
   ↓
Datagram
   ↓
Receiver

The sender can transmit a datagram without first establishing a transport connection.

docs.title: Datagram-Oriented
docs.text:
UDP preserves message/datagram boundaries.

If an application sends:

Message A
Message B

UDP treats these as separate datagrams.

This differs from TCP's byte-stream model.

Conceptually:

TCP
→ stream of bytes

UDP
→ individual datagrams

docs.title: No Built-In Delivery Guarantee
docs.text:
Suppose the sender sends:

Datagram 1
Datagram 2
Datagram 3

The network might deliver:

Datagram 1
Datagram 3

with Datagram 2 lost.

UDP itself does not automatically retransmit the lost datagram.

If the application requires retransmission, it must implement suitable logic itself or use a higher-level protocol that does so.

docs.title: No Built-In Ordering Guarantee
docs.text:
Suppose:

Sent:
1
2
3

The receiver might observe:

2
1
3

UDP does not reorder the datagrams for the application.

docs.title: TCP vs UDP
docs.text: TCP UDP Connection-oriented Connectionless Reliable transport mechanisms No delivery guarantee Ordered byte stream Independent datagrams Retransmission No built-in retransmission Flow control No TCP-style flow control Congestion mechanisms No TCP-style built-in behavior Higher protocol machinery Simpler transport

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Use TCP when you think:

I need a reliable ordered stream.

Think about UDP when:

I need datagrams with minimal transport machinery,
and the application/protocol can tolerate or manage loss.

Do not use:

TCP = slow
UDP = fast

as your mental model.

That is too simplistic.

The important difference is the transport guarantees and behavior.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
Many traditional DNS queries use UDP.

Conceptually:

Client
   ↓
DNS Query
   ↓
UDP
   ↓
DNS Server

DNS may use TCP in some circumstances as well.

Therefore avoid thinking:

DNS always uses only UDP.

docs.title: Real-Time Media
docs.text:
For live voice or video, receiving a very old packet may sometimes be less useful than continuing with newer data.

Example:

Live Audio

Packet 1
Packet 2
Packet 3 lost
Packet 4
Packet 5

The application may prefer continuing playback instead of stopping everything waiting for Packet 3.

Actual real-time systems are more sophisticated, but this illustrates the motivation.

docs.title: Online Gaming
docs.text:
Fast-changing game state can sometimes tolerate missing individual updates because a newer update may quickly replace an older one.

The exact protocol design depends on the game.

docs.title: QUIC
docs.text:
QUIC uses UDP as its transport foundation.

HTTP/3 runs over QUIC.

Conceptually:

HTTP/3
  ↓
QUIC
  ↓
UDP
  ↓
IP

QUIC implements sophisticated reliability, security, and multiplexing behavior above UDP.

Therefore:

UDP being underneath does not mean HTTP/3 itself is unreliable.

docs.title: UDP and Ports
docs.text:
UDP also uses port numbers.

Example:

Client
10.0.0.5:52000

        ↓ UDP

Server
10.0.0.10:53

Port 53 is commonly associated with DNS.

TCP port 53 and UDP port 53 are distinct transport endpoints because the protocol is part of the endpoint identity.

docs.title: Lab 1 — UDP Listener
docs.text:
On systems where your nc implementation supports it:

nc -u -l 9001

In another terminal:

nc -u localhost 9001

Type:

hello

Observe the received datagram data.

docs.title: Lab 2 — Compare TCP and UDP
docs.text:
TCP server:

nc -l 9000

TCP client:

nc localhost 9000

UDP server:

nc -u -l 9001

UDP client:

nc -u localhost 9001

The exercise is primarily to understand that the transport protocol can change while using the same general socket abstraction.

docs.title: Lab 3 — Inspect UDP Endpoints
docs.text:
On macOS:

lsof -iUDP -P -n

Observe processes using UDP sockets.

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
UDP offers:

  • small transport header
  • no connection handshake
  • message boundaries
  • application-controlled communication behavior

docs.title: Disadvantages
docs.text:
UDP does not directly provide:

  • delivery guarantee
  • ordering guarantee
  • retransmission
  • TCP-style flow control
  • TCP-style reliability semantics

If an application needs those features, it must provide them elsewhere.

docs.title: UDP Does Not Mean Bad or Unreliable Application
docs.text:
UDP itself does not guarantee delivery.

But applications and protocols built on UDP can implement reliability.

QUIC is an important example.

docs.title: UDP Is Not Always Faster
docs.text:
Performance depends on:

  • protocol design
  • network conditions
  • workload
  • application behavior

UDP has less built-in transport machinery, but that does not automatically mean every UDP application performs better than every TCP application.

docs.title: UDP Still Uses IP and Ports
docs.text:
Conceptually:

Application
   ↓
UDP
   ↓
IP
   ↓
Network

UDP does not replace IP.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
UDP has no built-in encryption.

Applications must use appropriate security protocols when confidentiality or authenticity is required.

UDP-based services can also be associated with amplification and spoofing risks when poorly designed.

Security specifics will be studied later.

docs.title: Performance Considerations
docs.text:
UDP avoids connection-establishment overhead at the transport layer.

This can be useful for certain workloads.

However applications may need additional logic for:

  • loss handling
  • ordering
  • retries
  • security
  • congestion management

The total system cost depends on the protocol built above UDP.

docs.title: Interview Questions
docs.text:
1. What is UDP?
  2. Why does UDP exist?
  3. What does connectionless mean?
  4. Is UDP reliable?
  5. Does UDP guarantee ordering?
  6. Does UDP retransmit lost data?
  7. What is a datagram?
  8. TCP stream vs UDP datagram?
  9. TCP vs UDP?
  10. When would UDP make sense?
  11. Why might real-time applications use UDP?
  12. Does DNS always use only UDP?
  13. Does UDP use ports?
  14. Is UDP encrypted?
  15. Why does HTTP/3 use UDP underneath?
  16. Does using UDP automatically make HTTP/3 unreliable?
  17. Can an application build reliability on top of UDP?
  18. Is UDP always faster than TCP?
  19. What information identifies a UDP endpoint?
  20. Where does UDP fit relative to IP?

docs.text:

docs.title: My Understanding
docs.text:
UDP is a connectionless transport protocol that sends independent datagrams between endpoints.

Unlike TCP, UDP does not provide built-in reliable delivery, ordering, retransmission, or connection establishment.

This simpler model can be useful when applications value timeliness, message-oriented communication, or want to implement their own transport behavior.

UDP is not automatically faster or better than TCP; the correct choice depends on application requirements.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
This guide defines how every note in the engineering-handbook repository should be written, formatted, organized, illustrated, and maintained.

The goal is to create notes that remain:

  • easy to understand
  • easy to revise
  • technically accurate
  • visually clean
  • interview friendly
  • useful during real engineering work
  • maintainable for many years

docs.title: 1. Core Rule
docs.text:
Every note should answer these questions:

  1. What is it?
  2. Why does it exist?
  3. What problem does it solve?
  4. How does it work?
  5. When should I use it?
  6. When should I not use it?
  7. What are the trade-offs?
  8. What can go wrong?
  9. How do I debug it?
  10. How would I explain it to another engineer?

Do not copy documentation.

Understand the concept first, then write it in your own words.

docs.title: 2. Standard Note Structure
docs.text:
Every technical topic should follow approximately this structure:

# Topic Name

> One-line summary of the topic.

## What is it?

## Why does it exist?

## Mental Model

## How does it work?

## Important Concepts

## Example

## When to Use

## When Not to Use

## Advantages

## Disadvantages

## Trade-offs

## Common Problems

## Debugging

## Security Considerations

## Performance Considerations

## Interview Questions

## My Understanding

## References

Not every section is mandatory.

Use only sections that actually add value.

docs.title: 3. Heading Rules
docs.text:
Use headings consistently.

# Topic

## Major Section

### Subsection

#### Small Detail

Recommended maximum depth:

#    Topic
##   Section
###  Subsection

Avoid using more than three heading levels unless absolutely necessary.

Never use headings only for visual styling.

docs.title: 4. Font
docs.text:
Do not define custom fonts.

GitHub automatically renders Markdown using its own readable interface fonts.

This means:

  • no custom font files
  • no embedded Google Fonts
  • no CSS font imports
  • no font-specific HTML unless absolutely necessary

The content should remain readable anywhere Markdown is rendered.

docs.title: 5. Font Size
docs.text:
Do not manually control font sizes.

Use Markdown hierarchy instead:

# Largest

## Large

### Medium

Normal text

Avoid:

<font size="..."> <span style="font-size:..."></span></font>

These reduce portability and often render inconsistently.

docs.title: 6. Colors
docs.text:
Avoid custom text colors.

Do not write notes like:

<span style="color:red">Important</span>

Instead use semantic markers.

Use:

✅ Correct
❌ Incorrect
⚠️ Warning
💡 Key idea
🔐 Security
🚀 Performance
🧠 Mental model
🐞 Debugging
🎯 Interview

Use emojis sparingly.

Recommended rule:

Maximum one icon per important section or concept.

Do not turn every bullet into an emoji.

docs.title: 7. Emphasis
docs.text:
Use bold for important terms.

HTTP is a **stateless application-layer protocol**.

Use italics only occasionally.

This behavior is _implementation dependent_.

Avoid excessive bolding.

Bad:

**HTTP** is a **PROTOCOL** used for **CLIENT SERVER COMMUNICATION**.

Good:

HTTP is a **request-response protocol** used between clients and servers.

docs.title: 8. One-Line Summary
docs.text:
Every note should begin with a simple summary.

Example:

# HTTP

> HTTP is an application-layer request-response protocol used for communication between clients and servers.

This becomes extremely useful during quick revision.

docs.title: 9. Mental Models
docs.text:
Every difficult concept should contain a simple mental model.

Example:

Client
   ↓
HTTP Request
   ↓
Server
   ↓
Business Logic
   ↓
Database
   ↓
HTTP Response
   ↓
Client

Mental models should be simple enough to remember.

Avoid overly detailed diagrams in the beginning.

docs.title: 10. Diagrams
docs.text:
Use diagrams whenever relationships or flow are easier to understand visually.

Preferred order:

  1. ASCII / text diagram
  2. Mermaid diagram
  3. Image only when necessary

docs.title: Simple diagrams
docs.text:
Prefer:

Browser
   ↓
DNS
   ↓
Server
   ↓
Database

For simple concepts, text diagrams are better than images.

They are:

  • searchable
  • editable
  • lightweight
  • version controlled
  • readable directly in GitHub

docs.title: 11. Mermaid Diagrams
docs.text:
Use Mermaid for architecture and more complex flows.

Example:

flowchart TD
    A[Browser] --> B[Load Balancer]
    B --> C[Node API]
    C --> D[Redis]
    C --> E[MongoDB]

Good uses:

  • architecture
  • request flows
  • sequences
  • database relationships
  • CI/CD flow
  • Kubernetes architecture
  • state transitions

Do not use Mermaid when a four-line ASCII diagram is enough.

docs.title: 12. Images
docs.text:
Images should only be added when they improve understanding.

Examples:

  • AWS architecture diagram
  • Kubernetes architecture
  • browser DevTools screenshot
  • Grafana dashboard explanation
  • database execution plan visualization

Do not add images only for decoration.

docs.title: 13. Image Directory Structure
docs.text:
Do not place images randomly inside folders.

Use:

assets/
├── networking/
├── system-design/
├── aws/
├── docker/
├── kubernetes/
├── databases/
└── frontend/

Example:

assets/networking/http-request-response.png

Reference it:

![HTTP request-response flow](../../assets/networking/http-request-response.png)

docs.title: 14. Image Naming
docs.text:
Use lowercase kebab-case.

Good:

http-request-response.png
aws-vpc-architecture.png
docker-networking.png
kubernetes-service-flow.png

Avoid:

Screenshot 2026-10-12.png
image1.png
final-image-new.png
diagram.png

The filename should explain what the image contains.

docs.title: 15. Image Format
docs.text:
Preferred:

.svg   diagrams/icons
.png   screenshots
.webp  large compressed images

Avoid large JPG files when unnecessary.

For diagrams, prefer SVG because it stays sharp at any size.

docs.title: 16. Screenshot Rules
docs.text:
When adding screenshots:

  • crop unnecessary browser/window areas
  • remove personal information
  • remove company information
  • remove credentials
  • remove tokens
  • remove internal URLs
  • remove customer data
  • remove account IDs

Add a short explanation immediately below the screenshot.

Never use a screenshot instead of explaining the concept.

docs.title: 17. Tables
docs.text:
Use tables for comparisons.

Example:

HTTP Method Purpose GET Read POST Create/process PUT Replace PATCH Partial update DELETE Delete

Tables are especially useful for:

  • comparisons
  • commands
  • status codes
  • cloud services
  • database differences
  • interview summaries

Avoid very large tables.

If a table has more than roughly 7–8 columns, rethink the structure.

docs.title: 18. Code Blocks
docs.text:
Always specify the language.

Good:

const user = await getUser(id);

curl https://example.com

services:
  api:
    image: my-api

Avoid:

const user = await getUser(id);

when it is actually code.

Syntax highlighting improves readability.

docs.title: 19. Code Example Rules
docs.text:
Every code example should demonstrate one idea.

Avoid pasting complete applications into notes.

Bad:

500-line Express application

Good:

app.get("/health", (req, res) => {
  res.status(200).json({ status: "ok" });
});

If the example requires a full project, place it under:

projects/

and link to it from the note.

docs.title: 20. Commands
docs.text:
Commands should always use shell blocks.

docker ps

If output matters:

CONTAINER ID   IMAGE      STATUS
abc123         node:20    Up 5 minutes

Keep command and output separate.

docs.title: 21. Definitions
docs.text:
Do not use dictionary-style definitions alone.

Bad:

Load balancer: distributes network traffic.

Better:

A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend instances so a single server does not become the bottleneck or single point of failure.

Then add:

Client
   ↓
Load Balancer
 ↙    ↓    ↘
API1 API2 API3

docs.title: 22. Real-World Examples
docs.text:
Every important topic should have at least one practical example.

Example:

## Real-World Example

Suppose one Node API instance can safely handle 1,000 requests per second.

If traffic increases to 5,000 requests per second, multiple instances can run behind a load balancer.

This converts theory into engineering understanding.

docs.title: 23. Trade-Offs
docs.text:
Senior-level notes must include trade-offs.

Example:

## Trade-offs

Redis caching improves latency and reduces database load.

However, it introduces:

- cache invalidation complexity
- additional infrastructure
- possible stale data
- memory cost

Avoid notes that make technologies look universally good.

docs.title: 24. "When Not to Use" Section
docs.text:
This is especially important.

Example:

## When Not to Use Redis

Do not introduce Redis only because the system might become slow someday.

Start with the database unless measurements show that caching is necessary.

Understanding when not to use something is often more senior than knowing how to use it.

docs.title: 25. Debugging Section
docs.text:
Whenever possible add:

## Debugging

Symptoms:

- API timeout
- high latency
- connection refused

Check:

1. Is the process running?
2. Is the port listening?
3. Can the service be reached?
4. Are logs showing errors?
5. Is the downstream dependency healthy?

Build a troubleshooting mindset.

docs.title: 26. Security Section
docs.text:
Add security considerations whenever relevant.

Example:

## Security Considerations

- Never send credentials over plain HTTP.
- Use HTTPS.
- Validate input.
- Protect authentication tokens.

docs.title: 27. Performance Section
docs.text:
Add performance considerations when meaningful.

Example:

## Performance Considerations

For high traffic:

- enable connection reuse
- avoid unnecessarily large payloads
- use compression appropriately
- cache static resources

docs.title: 28. Interview Questions
docs.text:
Each major topic should contain approximately 5–10 questions.

Example:

## Interview Questions

1. What is HTTP?
2. Why is HTTP stateless?
3. PUT vs PATCH?
4. 401 vs 403?
5. How does HTTP keep-alive work?

Do not immediately write answers underneath every question.

Attempt them from memory first.

docs.title: 29. My Understanding
docs.text:
This is the most important section.

At the bottom of every note:

## My Understanding

HTTP provides a standardized request-response communication model between a client and server.

The application decides what to do with the request; HTTP only defines how the messages are exchanged.

This section must always be written completely in your own words.

Update it as your understanding improves.

docs.title: 30. References
docs.text:
Every note should contain good primary references.

Example:

## References

- [MDN: HTTP Overview](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Overview)
- [RFC 9110: HTTP Semantics](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110)

Reference priority:

  1. Official documentation
  2. RFC / specification
  3. Vendor documentation
  4. High-quality engineering article
  5. Video/course

Avoid using random blogs as the primary technical authority.

docs.title: 31. File Naming
docs.text:
Use lowercase kebab-case.

Good:

http.md
http-caching.md
tcp-handshake.md
event-loop.md
database-indexes.md
horizontal-scaling.md

Avoid:

HTTP Notes.md
HttpCachingFinal.md
my_notes.md
topic1.md

docs.title: 32. Folder Naming
docs.text:
Use lowercase kebab-case.

Example:

system-design/
distributed-systems/
api-design/
operating-systems/

Do not mix:

SystemDesign/
system_design/
system-design/

Choose one convention and keep it forever.

Recommended:

lowercase kebab-case

docs.title: 33. Note Length
docs.text:
Do not optimize for short notes or long notes.

Optimize for usefulness.

Typical target:

Simple concept      → 50–150 lines
Medium concept      → 150–300 lines
Large topic         → split into multiple files

Instead of one huge:

aws.md

prefer:

aws/
├── iam.md
├── vpc.md
├── ec2.md
├── s3.md
├── cloudfront.md
└── load-balancing.md

docs.title: 34. Split Large Topics
docs.text:
One file should represent one logical topic.

Bad:

networking.md

containing HTTP, TCP, DNS, TLS, CDN, proxies, load balancers.

Better:

networking/
├── http.md
├── dns.md
├── tcp.md
├── tls.md
├── proxy.md
├── load-balancer.md
└── cdn.md

This improves search and revision.

docs.title: 35. Cross-Link Notes
docs.text:
Your handbook should become interconnected.

Example:

HTTP typically relies on TCP for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2.

See: [TCP](./tcp.md)

Later:

For caching strategies, see:
[Cache Aside](../../system-design/patterns/cache-aside.md)

Over time, the repository becomes your personal engineering wiki.

docs.title: 36. Use Relative Links
docs.text:
Prefer:

[DNS](./dns.md)

instead of links tied to GitHub URLs.

Relative links continue to work:

  • locally
  • on GitHub
  • if repository name changes
  • if repository becomes public/private

docs.title: 37. Callouts
docs.text:
GitHub supports useful blockquotes.

Use:

> [!NOTE]
> HTTP itself is stateless.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Never store passwords in plaintext.

> [!WARNING]
> Never commit AWS access keys.

> [!TIP]
> Use `curl -v` to inspect request and connection details.

Use callouts only for genuinely important information.

docs.title: 38. Do Not Overdecorate
docs.text:
Avoid:

  • excessive emojis
  • giant banners
  • GIFs
  • decorative screenshots
  • unnecessary badges
  • multiple text colors
  • huge ASCII art
  • unnecessary HTML
  • complicated CSS

The handbook should look like professional engineering documentation.

docs.title: 39. Suggested Visual Style
docs.text:
Use this visual hierarchy:

# Topic

> One-line summary.

Short introduction.

## Core Concept

Explanation.

### Example

Code/diagram.

## How It Works

Flow.

## Trade-offs

Table/list.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Important point.

## Interview Questions

Questions.

## My Understanding

Short final explanation.

## References

Sources.

This creates a predictable reading experience.

docs.title: 40. Status Metadata
docs.text:
Optionally place this near the top:

**Status:** 🟡 Learning  
**Last reviewed:** 2026-10-12  
**Confidence:** Beginner

Recommended confidence values:

Beginner
Comfortable
Strong
Needs Revision

Avoid percentages like:

HTTP — 63%

They are difficult to measure meaningfully.

docs.title: 41. Revision Dates
docs.text:
Use:

**Last reviewed:** 2026-10-12

Update it when you genuinely revise the topic.

This tells you which knowledge may have become stale.

This is especially useful for:

  • React
  • AWS
  • Kubernetes
  • Node.js
  • security
  • AI
  • cloud services

docs.title: 42. Git Commit Strategy
docs.text:
Commit notes based on meaningful learning.

Examples:

learn(networking): add HTTP request-response fundamentals

learn(networking): add DNS resolution notes

learn(docker): document container networking

lab(aws): add VPC experiment

revise(node): improve event loop explanation

fix(kubernetes): correct service networking notes

Avoid:

update notes
changes
new
final
final2

The Git history should tell the story of your learning.

docs.title: 43. Practical Labs
docs.text:
Theory files should live with practical experimentation.

Example:

fundamentals/networking/
├── http.md
├── dns.md
└── labs/
    ├── curl/
    └── node-http-server/

Or larger labs can live under:

projects/

Choose based on size.

docs.title: 44. Never Commit Secrets
docs.text:
Never include:

AWS keys
API tokens
JWT signing secrets
passwords
database credentials
company URLs
internal code
customer information
private certificates

Use:

YOUR_API_KEY
example.com
user@example.com

instead.

docs.title: 45. Sources of Images
docs.text:
When possible, create diagrams yourself.

If using external diagrams:

  • verify license
  • link to the original source
  • prefer official documentation
  • avoid copying copyrighted diagrams unnecessarily

For architecture diagrams, recreating the concept yourself is usually better because it proves understanding.

docs.title: 46. Recommended Diagram Tools
docs.text: Preferred:

docs.title: Mermaid
docs.text: Best for diagrams directly stored as text in Git.

docs.title: Excalidraw
docs.text:
Best for hand-drawn architecture explanations.

Store source files if useful:

diagrams/source/

and exported SVGs:

assets/system-design/

docs.title: draw.io
docs.text:
Useful for larger architecture diagrams.

Again, keep both source and exported version when worthwhile.

docs.title: 47. Diagram Naming Example
docs.text:
diagrams/
├── source/
│   └── url-shortener.drawio
│
└── exported/
    └── url-shortener.svg

Or:

assets/system-design/url-shortener.svg

docs.title: 48. Your Note-Writing Workflow
docs.text:
For every topic:

1. Read official material

        ↓

2. Understand concept

        ↓

3. Close documentation

        ↓

4. Write from memory

        ↓

5. Reopen reference

        ↓

6. Correct gaps

        ↓

7. Add example

        ↓

8. Add diagram

        ↓

9. Add trade-offs

        ↓

10. Add interview questions

        ↓

11. Write "My Understanding"

        ↓

12. Commit

The critical step is:

Close documentation before initially writing your explanation.

That prevents your notes from becoming copied documentation.

docs.title: 49. 80/20 Rule for Notes
docs.text:
Spend roughly:

70% learning / experimenting

30% documenting

Do not spend more time making the note beautiful than learning the concept.

Your handbook is a tool for engineering growth, not a design portfolio.

docs.title: 50. Definition of a Finished Note
docs.text:
A note is sufficiently complete when you can:

  • explain the concept without reading it
  • give a practical example
  • identify key trade-offs
  • identify common problems
  • answer its main interview questions
  • find additional detail quickly from references

A note does not need to contain everything known about the topic.

docs.title: Final Standard
docs.text:
Every good engineering note should make it possible to answer:

WHAT?
WHY?
HOW?
WHEN?
WHEN NOT?
TRADE-OFF?
FAILURE?
DEBUG?
EXAMPLE?
INTERVIEW?

If the note answers those clearly, it is useful.

If it only contains definitions copied from documentation, it is not.
